metadata.title: Evaluating the alignment between the Grade 9 mathematics Annual National Assessment (ANA) and TIMSS

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study does not use student-level microdata from TIMSS or ANA; instead, it purposively samples the Grade 9 mathematics ANA question papers (2012–2014) and the Grade 8 mathematics TIMSS 2011 response items, then constructs topic-by-cognitive-level matrices. Because the analysis is based on test specifications and frequency counts of mapped cells (rather than a representative student sample), the paper does not report the use of complex survey weights or any ILSA weight variables (e.g., student sampling weights). The alignment index (Porter’s alignment index) is computed from collapsed 4×4 matrices derived from the test content mapping, so weighting is not applicable to the estimation target. The only “preprocessing” described is the mapping by a panel of three reviewers and the collapsing of cells into a 4×4 matrix to compute alignment indices and mean deviations.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The study does not model cognitive achievement scores or any PV-based outcomes; it evaluates curriculum-to-assessment alignment using Porter’s alignment index computed from topic and cognitive-level matrices derived from test content. Since the dependent variable is an alignment metric (based on mapped frequencies/ratios), plausible values are not applicable. Missing-data handling is not reported because there is no missingness in PVs or student responses being imputed or deleted; the analysis is based on complete test-paper specifications and reviewer mappings.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Purposive sampling was used to select the Grade 9 mathematics ANA question papers for 2012 (n=59), 2013 (n=62), and 2014 (n=61), and the Grade 8 mathematics TIMSS response items for 2011 (n=90), based on access provided by the Department of Basic Education (DBE). The study then generated 4×4 topic-by-cognitive-level matrices by mapping ANA topics and cognitive levels (from the SAGM and CAPS-aligned framework) and TIMSS topics and cognitive levels (from the 2011 TIMSS mathematics framework) into four collapsed topic categories and four cognitive-level categories. A panel of three mathematics-education lecturers mapped the topics and cognitive levels to record matches (hits) in the matrix cells; interrater reliability was reported as 0.96. No student-level inclusion/exclusion, missing-response filtering, or PV-based scoring procedures are described because the unit of analysis is the test content mapping and resulting alignment indices.

The analysis uses ANA question papers from 2012 (n=59), 2013 (n=62), and 2014 (n=61) and TIMSS 2011 response items (n=90), mapped by three reviewers into collapsed 4×4 matrices. The Porter’s alignment index indicates moderate-to-perfect alignment overall but still reveals substantial misalignment: 0.657 (34.3% misalignment) for 2012, 0.728 (27.2% misalignment) for 2013, and 0.681 (31.9% misalignment) for 2014. The study also reports mean deviations showing which topic and cognitive-level cells were preferred or underrepresented, with ANA showing irregular cognitive-level testing across years. Limitations include the absence of student-level PV achievement modeling and no ML prediction pipeline; the results are alignment-based and do not establish causal effects on learner performance. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: This is an alignment study based on test-content mapping and computation of Porter’s alignment index, not an empirical machine-learning prediction study. Consequently, there are no ML algorithms, no PV-based achievement outcomes, and no student-level weighting or missing-data procedures to extract. The paper reports alignment indices and descriptive deviations derived from frequency/ratio matrices rather than predictive performance metrics.
